accuracy.evidence: Terms and structure follow Common Core ELA SL.4.3 (identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points) and the English National Curriculum spoken-language strand (listen and respond, ask relevant questions). Point/claim, reason and evidence are used as in standard argument-writing guidance: the reason answers why, evidence is a fact, number, example or sourced statement. Signal words (because, for example, according to, so) are labelled with the role they usually signal, and each logic card has one clear fault.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: calling an example a reason (the beans line), accepting any sentence on the same topic as support ('I really love lunch', 'Pizza is the best lunch'), treating opinion as evidence ('Blue is the best colour'), over-generalising from two cases ('so everyone finds assembly boring'), a point that does not follow ('We won the match, so a longer lunch'), and asking follow-ups that do not test the claim.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built around analysing a spoken argument: tagging each line of one council talk as point, reason or evidence with running counts, tapping signal words inside a sentence, a relevance sort against a stated point, naming the fault in weak reasoning, and choosing a probing question. Building on Others (flagbuildon) is about extending replies and Textual Evidence (flagevid) is about quoting from a text; the shingle gate passed against all flagship labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner first builds the structure of a talk (1 point, 2 reasons, 2 pieces of evidence), then learns the cues that reveal it, then judges whether claims support the point, then judges whether the reasoning holds, and finally turns that judgement into a question, which matches the three evidence statements for this topic (list reasons and evidence, evaluate logic and relevance, ask probing follow-up questions).

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: 'A reason' for an example (disproved when it only fits Evidence), 'Yes, it is about lunch' for an off-the-point claim (disproved in the relevance sort), and 'Strong: it has a reason' for an over-generalisation (disproved when it lands in Too few examples).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with nine distinct m= messages naming the slip: the point picked instead of the reason, one word mistaken for a reason, the signal word mistaken for the evidence, same-topic but off-the-point claims, a personal anecdote, 'having a so is not enough', misreading the point, a question about liking rather than evidence, and repeating instead of probing.

readability.evidence: Learner text reads at FK 3.4 (limit 6.5) and adult text at FK 6.2 (limit 9.5) after splitting long sentences. Speech lines are short school-council sentences a 9-year-old would hear; canvas headings are one line; zone labels are one to three words.

no_filler.evidence: Passes the filler regex and 12% duplicate gate. Kid paragraphs cover point, reason and evidence, signal words, and judging; adult paragraphs cover the standard and terms, how to scaffold listening, the named mistakes with a 'because' check, and what the lab does. Each lab step has a separate job.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots of every step before and after Show me: the speech card wraps to two or three lines, the three tag zones and the 2 × 2 logic grid fit at 390 px, the signal-word chips wrap onto three rows with room to tap, and the question cards stack. The challenge answer buttons wrap without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes and there are no console errors. Every drag has a button route (Point/Reason/Evidence, one button per word, Supports/Off the point, the four logic verdicts, the three questions) and the canvas aria-label gives the feedback after every choice.

sources: Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, SL.4.3 (identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points)
Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: spoken language, years 1 to 6
Voice 21 / Oracy Cambridge, The Oracy Framework (reasoning and evidence strand)
